Input: Why are there so many people who pick Michael Jordan and other, newer players as the basketball GOAT over Wilt Chamberlain? It seems undeniable that Wilt Chamberlain is the basketball GOAT, but as one of my favorite sages pointed out: “Denial ain’t just a river in Egypt.” — Mark Twain Many human beings live in denial of obvious things, saying the earth is flat, vaccines are more dangerous than the diseases they combat, etc. And many basketball fans are in denial about Wilt Chamberlain, the obvious basketball GOAT. For six years in his prime, Wilt Chamberlain averaged around 40 points, 25 rebounds and 8.8 blocks per game, while leading the NBA in field goal percentage nine out of the 13 years he played. No other volume scorer of Wilt’s magnitude led the league in field goal percentage nine times, and Michael Jordan, LeBron James and Kobe Bryant never led the league once, or even came close. And yet Wilt was accused of “scoring too much.” Why? Why was a far less efficient scorer, Michael Jordan, praised for his scoring, while a far more efficient scorer was damned? As Wilt pointed out himself, “Nobody pulls for Goliath.” Wilt changed his game to pass more and score less, by giving the ball to less efficient shooters, and he became the first and only center to lead the league in assists. What did the basketball world do? It continued to play favorites. MJ was a guard but he never led the league in assists, nor did Kobe. In what way were they “better” than Wilt? Championships are team accomplishments. MJ was 1-9 in the playoffs and 0-6 against the Larry Bird Celtics, back when the Celtics, Pistons and Lakers had super teams. MJ only started winning rings when the superteams declined and his Bulls added championship-level teammates like Scottie Pippen, Horace Grant and B.J. Armstrong. MJ only won rings when he had the best team. His teams struggled mightily in the playoffs when other teams were better. Ironically, Michael Jordan is the best argument against using rings to determine the GOAT. by Michael R. Burch

How does Larry Holmes’ legacy change if he never beat up an old Ali? What do you think? Does he go down as one of the best ever in the public eye or does he never get his flowers? If Larry Holmes had not defeated an aging Ali, I think it would drop him a bit in the all-time rankings. This is how I rank the all-time heavyweights. Then I will discuss Holmes and the possible effects of a loss to Ali. THE TOP 25 HEAVYWEIGHTS OF ALL TIME by Michael R. Burch What would have happened if Larry Holmes had lost to an aging Ali? I see two very different outcomes. Holmes could have recovered to go 68-7, perhaps slipping to around #14 in my ranking. People who were around in 1974, who did you pick to win Ali vs Foreman? Nearly everyone picked George Foreman to defeat Muhammad Ali in the infamous “Rumble in the Jungle”. And there were widespread fears that the fearsome Foreman would seriously injure the aging and seemingly washed-up Ali. The 1974 fight was hardly seen as a clash of ring Titans. Foreman and his camp were all smiles before the overhyped “rumble,” confident of victory. An easy victory, like 40 others. On the other hand Ali was 32 and had lost the fabulous speed that had once set him apart from other heavyweights. Furthermore, the older, slower, underpowered Ali had lost to two boxers Foreman had demolished via second-round knockouts: Joe Frazier and Ken Norton. When Ali managed to come back and win the rematches, it was by the skin of his teeth. There simply was no comparison between the much younger, in-his-prime, more powerful Foreman and the much diminished Ali. With the benefit of perfect hindsight, we forget how far Ali had fallen from grace in the eyes of the boxing world. Ali’s heyday had ended seven years prior — an eternity in boxing years. Ali had dominated the heavyweight division from 1964 to 1967, but that was ancient history. What had he done for boxing fans lately, other than lose to and eke out narrow victories over his best opponents? After fighting the diminished Ali in 1970, when he was three years past his prime, Jerry Quarry said: “He’s still damn good, but he ain’t what he was. If you want to see Ali when he was Ali, watch the Cleveland Williams fight. And the much-prophesied Stumble in the Jungle was seven years past Ali’s prime. Ali still talked a good fight, but the boxing world was not impressed and predicted consensus doom for the all-talk Louisville Lip. The only question was how long Ali could last before Foreman knocked him out. Could he make it past the second round, even? Almost no one associated with boxing, not even Ali's long-time friend and supporter Howard Cosell, gave the fast-fading former champion a plugged nickel’s chance of winning. Younger, more formidable boxers had failed to do so for three years prior to the 1974 mismatch! Foreman was a brooding and intimidating presence — a bigger, scarier Mike Tyson — who seemed invincible. He was 40-0 with a staggering 37 knockouts, please pardon the pun. He had a 92.5% knockout rate. No fighter had ever gone more than 10 rounds with Foreman, and only three of those. Fearsome Foreman had a string of 24 consecutive knockouts and in his previous 12 fights only one boxer had made it past the second round. Luis Faustino Pires managed to eke into the fourth round before getting destroyed. In those 12 fights, Foreman’s opponents averaged exactly 2.0 rounds per match. Foreman’s ability to knock out quality opponents so quickly was unprecedented in boxing history. Foreman was a juggernaut. And he was in his prime at age 25, seven years younger than Ali. Howard Cosell predicted doom for the underpowered, washed up Ali. So did professional oddsmakers. There were rumors that Ali’s camp feared for his health, perhaps even for his life. Ali put up a brave front, but nearly everyone thought it was all for show. He would collect a nice fat paycheck, then fade into obscurity, as past-their-prime heavyweights who hung on too long invariably do. At this stage of his career, Ali was more celebrity poet than a legitimate challenger to Foreman’s heavyweight belt, mantle and crown. All the charismatic Ali could do was charm the media and adoring Zaire crowds with amusing rhymes: "If you think the world was surprised when Nixon resigned, wait till I whup Foreman's behind!" "I've done something new for this fight. I done wrestled with an alligator, done tussled with a whale; handcuffed lightning, throw’d thunder in jail; only last week, I murdered a rock, injured a stone, hospitalized a brick; I'm so mean I make medicine sick." Of course Ali proved the world wrong and confirmed that he was, indeed, The Greatest, with a capital “T” and capital “G.” by Michael R. The birth of the love goddess Venus was similar to that of the biblical god Yahweh — in the endlessly fertile human imagination. THE BIRTH AND EVOLUTION OF THE BIBLICAL GODS by Michael R. Burch The biblical gods Yahweh/Jehovah and later Jesus and the mysterious Holy Ghost, are derivatives of several different gods and demigods, some of them Semitic and some from other areas of the world. This is how the biblical gods evolved over time… In the beginning was the supreme semitic god El, his consort Asherah, the Queen of Heaven, and his 70 sons and daughters, the Elohim. These names appear prominently throughout the Bible and we find the name of the supreme god El appearing in important names like Isra-el, Dani-el, Samu-el, and my own name, Micha-el, which means “Who is like El.” It is important to note that Elohim is obviously plural when used with plural verbs. Thus in the Genesis creation account we have the supreme god El saying to his sons and daughters the Elohim: “Let us (plural) make mankind in our (plural) own image” and we have the narrator saying, in the original text, “The gods (plural) made mankind in their (plural) own image, male and female created they (plural) them.” Once we understand the original concept, it makes perfect sense that men were created in the image of the male Elohim, while women were created in the image of the female Elohim. PHASE Ia: POLYTHEISM I will begin with polytheism prior to the creation of the Bible. The belief in gods probably began with a sense of awe, as primitive human beings observed the sun, moon, planets and stars with a sense of wonder and felt the tremendous effects of earthquakes, hurricanes and volcanoes. At times Nature seemed benevolent, but at other times Nature seemed angry, sometimes murderously angry. Nature seemed temperamental, like human beings. Thus it was natural for human beings to anthropomorphize Nature, creating human-like gods in the process. Nature in its various manifestations became the first gods: When Nature was angry, could the gods be appeased with offerings? Sometimes when offerings were made to the gods, good things happened. Thus the gods obviously liked human worship, praise and offerings. But when offerings were made and good things didn’t happen, did the gods want something more than ordinary food? Did they want enemies to be sacrificed? Or virgins? Or children? Even the king’s own son? Religion could quickly become a very bloody business. Meanwhile, witchdoctors who claimed to know how to intercede with the gods could make comfy livings without working like everyone else. When their “magic” didn’t work, they would inform the gullible that they hadn’t offered enough, or were too “sinful,” or some other claptrap. If prostitution is the oldest profession, religion is the most devious and the most profitable. PHASE Ib: POLYTHEISM PRODUCES PANTHEONS The next step in polytheism was the creation of pantheons of gods with specific pecking orders. Typically there was a supreme god like El, Zeus or Odin, then a hierarchy of more powerful and less powerful gods, followed by demigods who were half-human/half-divine, like Achilles and Heracles. Is William Wordsworth out of fashion? Far less people seem to care about him than Blake nowadays. Both William Blake and William Wordsworth remain influential today, albeit in different ways. William Blake has had the greater influence on modern thinking and culture: for instance, through his anti-establishment, reform-minded, free-thinking influence on singer-songwriters like Bob Dylan, John Lennon and Jim Morrison of the Doors. The Doors were named after Blake’s “doors of perception.” When Dylan met the Beatles for the first time and things were a bit icy at first, the poet Allen Ginsberg broke the ice by bringing up William Blake. It turned out that both Dylan and the Beatles were enthusiastic fans of Blake. William Wordsworth has had the greater influence on how poetry is written. His elegant blank verse has been a touchstone for many poets who followed him. Notable poets influenced by Wordsworth include his friend and sometimes partner Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Percy Bysshe Shelley (esp. “The Sunset,” “Alastor,” “Hymn to Intellectual Beauty” and “Mont Blanc”), John Keats (esp. “I stood tip-toe upon a little hill” and "Sleep and Poetry"), Lord Byron (less so, but in spots), Alfred Tennyson (in spots, esp. “Dora”), Walt Whitman (like Wordsworth a pantheist), Matthew Arnold (in spots, esp. “The Hayswater Boat”), Robert Frost (blank verse), Hart Crane (blank verse), Wallace Stevens (blank verse) and Elizabeth Bishop. Wordsworth also resurrected the sonnet, which had fallen into neglect, and thus influenced notable penners of sonnets such as Keats, Shelley, Tennyson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Christina Rossetti, Edgar Allan Poe, Gerard Manley Hopkins, Edna St. Vincent Millay and e. e. cummings. Wordsworth continues to influence writers, even if they don’t recognize his influence, via his ideas about writing poetry that he and Coleridge jointly expressed in the preface to Lyrical Ballads. These ideas include the communication of emotion recollected in tranquility; using the actual language being spoken rather than a highly ornate art-ificial (if you’ll pardon the pun) language; and dealing with the real world, common things and commoners, rather than kings, lords and heroes of yore.

God began and was born as a vague concept, then evolved into thousands of very different beings. I will trace the evolution of the biblical gods (yes, there were more than one) … PHASE Ia: POLYTHEISM I will begin with polytheism prior to the creation of the Bible. The belief in gods probably began with a sense of awe, as primitive human beings observed the sun, moon, planets and stars and felt the tremendous effects of earthquakes, hurricanes and volcanoes. At times Nature seemed benevolent. At other times Nature seemed angry, sometimes murderously angry. Nature seemed temperamental, like human beings. Thus it was natural for human beings to anthropomorphize Nature, creating human-like gods in the process. Nature in its various manifestations became the first gods: When Nature was angry, could the gods be appeased with offerings? Sometimes when offerings were made to the gods, good things happened. Thus the gods obviously liked human worship, praise and offerings. When offerings were made and good things didn’t happen, did the gods want something other than ordinary food? Did they want enemies to be sacrificed? Or virgins? Or children? Religion could become a very bloody business. Meanwhile, witchdoctors who claimed to know how to intercede with the gods could make a comfy living without working like everyone else. When their “magic” didn’t work, they would tell the gullible that they hadn’t offered enough, or were too “sinful,” or some other claptrap. If prostitution is the oldest profession, religion is the most devious and the most profitable. PHASE Ib: POLYTHEISM PRODUCES PANTHEONS The next step in polytheism was the creation of pantheons of gods with specific pecking orders. Typically there was a supreme god like Zeus or Odin, then a hierarchy of more powerful and less powerful gods, followed by demigods who were half-human/half-divine, like Achilles and Heracles. In some cases rulers were seen as gods or demigods. PHASE Ic: POLYTHEISM and the BIBLE According to Aaron Brody, a professor of Bible and archaeology at the Pacific School of Religion, the ancient Israelites were polytheists, "with only a small minority worshiping Yahweh alone before the historic events of 586 BC." In that year, the Judean elite were exiled to Babylon and the Jerusalem temple was destroyed. According to Brody this led to "a more universal vision of strict monotheism: one god not only for Judah, but for all the nations." In the beginning of the Bible there was El, the Sky God, and his 70 sons and daughters, the Elohim, who together formed a pantheon of gods widely worshipped throughout ancient Mesopotamia. This family of gods, the Elohim, a plural term used repeatedly throughout the Bible, is why El said, “Let us [plural] create mankind in our [plural] own image.” And it’s why the following verse says, “So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” Unless God is a hermaphrodite, he was speaking to male and female gods. For example the Bible’s alleged wisest man, King Solomon, built altars to other gods (1 Kings 11: 5-7). Nor was Yahweh all-powerful, since other tribes had competing deities. For example, in an amusing Bible verse, Yahweh was unable to defeat plains-dwellers who had iron chariots! Yahweh had to stick to the mountains, but was also unable to defeat the Jebusites who controlled Jerusalem. Other tribes had more powerful gods, apparently. PHASE II: GET RIDDA THE CHICK! Enheduanna, the daughter of the famous King Sargon the Great of Akkad, is the first ancient writer whose name remains known today. Not that you could endure God's voice—far from it! But heed the wind’s voice and the ceaseless formless message of silence: It murmurs now of the martyred young. Whenever you attended a church in Naples or Rome, didn't they come quietly to address you? And didn’t an exalted inscription impress its mission upon you recently, on the plaque in Santa Maria Formosa? What they require of me is that I gently remove any appearance of injustice— which at times slightly hinders their souls from advancing. Of course, it is endlessly strange to no longer inhabit the earth; to relinquish customs one barely had the time to acquire; not to see in roses and other tokens a hopeful human future; no longer to be oneself, cradled in infinitely caring hands; to set aside even one's own name, forgotten as easily as a child’s broken plaything. How strange to no longer desire one's desires! How strange to see meanings no longer cohere, drifting off into space. Dying is difficult and requires retrieval before one can gradually decipher eternity. The living all err in believing the too-sharp distinctions they create themselves. Angels (men say) don't know whether they move among the living or the dead. The eternal current merges all ages in its maelstrom until the voices of both realms are drowned out in its thunderous roar. In the end, the early-departed no longer need us: they are weaned gently from earth's agonies and ecstasies, as children outgrow their mothers’ breasts. But we, who need such immense mysteries, and for whom grief is so often the source of our spirit's progress— how can we exist without them? Is the legend of the lament for Linos meaningless— the daring first notes of the song pierce our apathy; then, in the interlude, when the youth, lovely as a god, has suddenly departed forever, we experience the emptiness of the Void for the first time— that harmony which now enraptures and comforts and aids us? Second Elegy by Rainer Maria Rilke loose translation/interpretation by Michael R. Burch Every angel is terrifying. And yet, alas, I invoke you, one of the soul’s lethal raptors, well aware of your nature. As in the days of Tobias, when one of you, obscuring his radiance, stood at the simple threshold, appearing ordinary rather than appalling while the curious youth peered through the window. But if the Archangel emerged today, perilous, from beyond the stars and took even one step toward us, our hammering hearts would pound us to death. What are you? Who are you? Joyous from the beginning; God’s early successes; Creation’s favorites; creatures of the heights; pollen of the flowering godhead; cusps of pure light; stately corridors; rising stairways; exalted thrones; filling space with your pure essence; crests of rapture; shields of ecstasy; storms of tumultuous emotions whipped into whirlwinds ... until one, acting alone, recreates itself by mirroring the beauty of its own countenance. While we, when deeply moved, evaporate; we exhale ourselves and fade away, growing faint like smoldering embers; we drift away like the scent of smoke. And while someone might say: “You’re in my blood! You occupy this room! You fill this entire springtime!” ... Still, what becomes of us? We cannot be contained; we vanish whether inside or out. And even the loveliest, who can retain them? Resemblance ceaselessly rises, then is gone, like dew from dawn’s grasses. And what is ours drifts away, like warmth from a steaming dish. O smile, where are you bound? O heavenward glance: are you a receding heat wave, a ripple of the heart? Alas, but is this not what we are? Does the cosmos we dissolve into savor us? Do the angels reabsorb only the radiance they emitted themselves, or sometimes, perhaps by oversight, traces of our being as well? Are we included in their features, as obscure as the vague looks on the faces of pregnant women? Do they notice us at all (how could they) as they reform themselves? Lovers, if they only knew how, might mutter marvelous curses into the night air. For it seems everything eludes us. See: the trees really do exist; our houses stand solid and firm. And yet we drift away, like weightless sighs. And all creation conspires to remain silent about us: perhaps from shame, perhaps some inexpressible hope? Lovers, gratified by each other, I ask to you consider: You cling to each other, but where is your proof of a connection? Sometimes my hands become aware of each other and my time-worn, exhausted face takes shelter in them, creating a slight sensation. But because of that, can I still claim to be? You, the ones who writhe with each other’s passions until, overwhelmed, someone begs: “No more!...”; You who swell beneath each other’s hands like autumn grapes; You, the one who dwindles as the other increases: I ask you to consider ... I know you touch each other so ardently because each caress preserves pure continuance, like the promise of eternity, because the flesh touched does not disappear. And yet, when you have survived the terror of initial intimacy, the first lonely vigil at the window, the first walk together through the blossoming garden: lovers, do you not still remain who you were before? If you lift your lips to each other’s and unite, potion to potion, still how strangely each drinker eludes the magic. Weren’t you confounded by the cautious human gestures on Attic gravestones? Weren’t love and farewell laid so lightly on shoulders they seemed composed of some ethereal substance unknown to us today? Consider those hands, how weightlessly they rested, despite the powerful torsos. The ancient masters knew: “We can only go so far, in touching each other. The gods can exert more force. But that is their affair.” If only we, too, could discover such a pure, contained Eden for humanity, our own fruitful strip of soil between river and rock. For our hearts have always exceeded us, as our ancestors’ did. And we can no longer trust our own eyes, when gazing at godlike bodies, our hearts find a greater repose.

What statistics distinguish a good MLB starting pitcher from an elite one? What are the benchmarks for greatness in this position? I believe the main purpose of a MLB pitcher is run prevention, so my “most vital” stats are: ERA+ and ERA I favor ERA+ because a 4.00 ERA in a high offense era may be better than a 3.50 ERA in a low offense era. ERA+ and ERA tell us that pitchers like Jack Morris and Bartolo Colon are questionable for the Hall of Fame, while pitchers like Smoky Joe Wood, Curt Schilling and Kevin Brown deserve strong consideration for inclusion. But we need to keep in mind that all defenses are not created equal. Great defenses can help prevent runs and make pitchers look better than they are. Poor defenses can make them look worse. Thus we need to consider: WHIP FIP The great Smoky Joe Wood remains an ultra-strong 17th in WHIP, a hundred years later. Tommy Bond is 20th. A fellow you may have heard of, Babe Ruth, remains in the top 100. How great, you may ask, was Smoky Joe Wood, really? Well, he’s fifth in FIP, just behind Satchel Paige and comfortably ahead of Walter Johnson, who once observed that no one ever threw faster than Smoky Joe. Tommy Bond is 10th in FIP. Babe Ruth is 76th. How tough is it to crack the top 100? Bob Gibson is 102nd and Pedro Martinez 111th. That tough. However, there are factors ERA+ and ERA, don’t tell us, such as how many innings a pitcher threw, helping to save the arms of the other pitchers on his team in the process. Thus my next “most vital” stat is: WAR WAR tells us that “inning eating” pitchers like Luis Tiant, Rick Reuschel, Wilbur Wood and Tommy John were better than their raw ERAs. I’m more of a peak performance fan than a longevity fan, so another stat I pay close attention to is: WAR7 WAR7 tells us that pitchers who deserve strong consideration for the HOF include Wes Ferrell (who is #26 and helped by his non-pitcher-like hitting), Curt Schilling, Wilbur Wood, Kevin Brown, and inning-heavy oldtimers like Jim McCormick (#7) and Tommy Bond (#14) who are increasingly difficult to compare to modern inning-light starters. Top 5 finishes in seasonal WAR, along with a high WAR7, help me identify undervalued “high peak” pitchers. TOP 5 Pitchers not in the HOF who have four or more finishes in the Top 5 in seasonal WAR include Wes Ferrell and Noodles Hahn (not eligible for the HOF because he only played 8 seasons). And leading old-timey pitchers is Jim McCormick. S-JAWS S-JAWS is a special calculation for starters that attempts to “normalize” for the crazy innings pitched by old-timey starters. But even with this revised calculation Jim McCormick is #35 and comparable to Wes Ferrell, Kevin Brown, Luis Tiant and Rick Reuschel. Several advanced stats keep telling me that these pitchers are top 30-60 and all belong in the HOF. Curt Schilling is an ultra-strong #23 here. David Cone is top 50. It is difficult to compare relievers to starters with stats like WAR and WAR7, so for relievers I consider a combination of: ERA+ and ERA, but these can be misleading in innings with inherited outs. WHIP FIP SAVES R-JAWS Which relievers deserve the most consideration for the HOF? Billy Wagner is sixth in R-JAWS and eighth in saves. Joe Nathan is seventh in R-JAWS and tenth in saves. They lead my reliever candidates for the HOF. In conclusion, after adding everything up, the ten pitchers I would vote for on a HOF ballot include Curt Schilling, Kevin Brown, Rick Reuschel, Luis Tiant, Wes Ferrell, Smoky Joe Wood, Wilbur Wood, David Cone and old-timers Jim McCormick and Tommy Bond. It bears noting that Ferrell and Wood were two of the best-hitting MLB pitchers not named Babe Ruth or Shohei Ohtani. And I will note that the only pitcher on my list that I am really a fan of, is Smoky Joe Wood. The others were all selected with complete objectivity. Honorable Mentions go to Joe Nathan, Nap Rucker, Bret Saberhagen, Johan Santana, Urban Shocker and Billy Wagner. by Michael R. Burch
